extraction.name: CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100
extraction.description: CIFAR-10 consists of 60000 32x32 colour images in 10 classes, with 6000 images per class. There are 50000 training images and 10000 test images. CIFAR-100 has 100 classes containing 600 images each. There are 500 training images and 100 testing images per class. The 100 classes in CIFAR-100 are grouped into 20 superclasses.
extraction.creator: Alex Krizhevsky
extraction.citeAs: Learning Multiple Layers of Features from Tiny Images, Alex Krizhevsky, 2009
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The tiny images dataset was collected by colleagues at MIT and NYU over the span of six months by searching the web for images of every non-abstract English noun in the lexical database WordNet. They used several search engines, including Google, Flickr, and Altavista and kept roughly the first 3000 results for each search term. After collecting all the images for a particular search term, they removed perfect duplicates and images in which an excessively large portion of the pixels were white. The dataset contains 80 million colour images downscaled to 32x32 and spread out across 79000 search terms.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images were collected from the web using search engines including Google, Flickr, and Altavista by searching for every non-abstract English noun in WordNet. Roughly the first 3000 results for each search term were kept.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: After collection, perfect duplicates were removed and images in which an excessively large portion of the pixels were white were removed as they tended to be synthetic figures rather than natural images. All images were downscaled to 32x32 pixels. Duplicate images were removed by comparing images with the L2 norm and using a rejection threshold liberal enough to capture not just perfect duplicates but also re-saved JPEGs.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images were downscaled to 32x32 pixels. For some experiments, data was whitened using the ZCA whitening transformation. The 1000 least-significant directions of variance were deleted from the dataset by setting to zero those entries of the diagonal matrix that correspond to the 1000 least significant principal components. The dataset was divided into training and test sets, with the training set receiving a randomly-selected 5000 images from each class for CIFAR-10.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Students were paid to label a subset of the tiny images dataset. Each labeler was given a class and asked to examine all the images which were found with that class as the search term. Labelers were also asked to examine all the images which were found with a search term that is a hyponym (as defined by WordNet) of the main search term. Labelers were instructed to reject images which did not belong to their assigned class. Criteria included: the class name should be high on the list of likely answers to 'What is in this picture?', the image should be photo-realistic, the image should contain only one prominent instance of the object, and the object may be partially occluded or seen from an unusual viewpoint as long as its identity is still clear. All labels submitted by labelers were personally verified.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: All labels submitted by the labelers were personally verified by the researchers.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: CIFAR-100 includes a 'people' superclass with classes: baby, boy, girl, man, woman, which may contain sensitive human attributes related to age and gender.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The search term used to find an image provides it with a rough label, although it is extremely unreliable due to the nature of online image search technology. Images tend to be symmetric about the vertical and horizontal, probably caused by the way people take photographs - making the ground plane horizontal and centering on the main object.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The labels from the original web search are extremely unreliable. The dataset consists of very small 32x32 images which limits the level of detail available. Some classes may be confused with each other (e.g., cats are frequently mistaken for dogs). Animals are seldom mistaken for non-animals and vice versa.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is suitable for unsupervised training of deep generative models and object recognition experiments. CIFAR-10 was used for training classifiers and testing the usefulness of features learned by RBMs. The labeled subsets (CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100) were created to enable object classification experiments. The dataset was divided into training and test sets for supervised learning tasks.
